title: The Nine Atonement Theories in Plain Words
question: Christians agree that Jesus' death and resurrection save us. So why are there so many theories about how it works, and what does each one actually say?
plainAnswer: The New Testament never gives one tidy explanation of how the cross saves. It uses many pictures side by side: a sacrifice, a ransom, a victory, a court verdict, a healing, a reconciled friendship. Over two thousand years Christians have built these pictures into fuller 'theories', each starting from a different answer to the question 'what is humanity's main problem?' No church council ever made one theory official for all Christians, so Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions emphasise different ones. Most teachers today hold that several theories capture something true; the real argument is about which one is the centre that holds the others together.
keyTakeaways: Each theory begins from a diagnosis: if the problem is slavery, the cure is rescue; if it is guilt, the cure is a verdict; if it is sickness, the cure is healing.
No ecumenical council defined a single theory of the atonement, unlike the councils that defined the Trinity and the person of Christ.

The early church mostly spoke of recapitulation, ransom, victory and healing; satisfaction (1098) and penal substitution (Reformation) were later systematic developments, though their roots are disputed.
Most theories cite real biblical texts; the disagreement is about which texts are central and which are illustrations.
Many writers today speak of a 'kaleidoscope' of images; others reply that one model, usually penal substitution or Christus Victor, must anchor the rest.
Common caricatures (God as an angry father, the cross as only an example, a deal struck with the devil) usually misrepresent what each theory's best defenders actually say.

sections.heading: What 'atonement' means
sections.body:
The English word 'atonement' is built from 'at one' plus '-ment': being made at one again with God. It became standard through early English Bibles; the King James Version uses it in Romans 5:11, where Paul says we have 'received the atonement' (modern versions say 'reconciliation').

In the Old Testament the main Hebrew verb is kipper, usually translated 'make atonement'. It is used above all of the Day of Atonement, when the high priest sprinkled blood and sent a goat into the wilderness to carry away Israel's sins (Leviticus 16). Scholars debate whether kipper means 'cover', 'wipe clean' or 'pay a ransom price'; it may carry all three shades in different places.

In the New Testament several word-families do the work: hilasterion and hilasmos (the 'mercy seat' or 'propitiation/expiation'), lytron (ransom), katallage (reconciliation) and dikaioo (to justify, declare in the right). Each word comes from a different area of life: the temple, the slave market, broken friendships, the law court. That variety is the seed of the later theories.

sources.author: Leon Morris
sources.title: The Apostolic Preaching of the Cross

sources.author: Jacob Milgrom
sources.title: Leviticus 1-16 (Anchor Bible)
sources.locator: comments on Lev 16 and the meaning of kipper

callout.text: Hilasterion in Romans 3:25 is translated 'propitiation' (turning away wrath) in the KJV and ESV, 'expiation' (wiping away sin) in the RSV, and 'sacrifice of atonement' in the NIV. C. H. Dodd argued for expiation in 1931; Leon Morris argued for propitiation in 1955. Both sides still have defenders.

sections.heading: Why there are many theories, not one
sections.body:
The early church fought hard over who Jesus is. The councils of Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) defined that he is fully God and fully human. They did not define how his death saves. The Nicene Creed simply says he came down 'for us and for our salvation' and was crucified 'for us'. That left room for many explanations.

The New Testament itself mixes images freely. In a single letter Paul can speak of redemption, sacrifice, justification and reconciliation within a few verses. Hebrews leans on the temple; Revelation on the victorious Lamb; John on being drawn and given life.

A 'theory' is what happens when a teacher takes one of these images and asks: what was wrong, what did Jesus do about it, and why did that work? The answers depend on the diagnosis. If the deepest problem is slavery to evil powers, the cure is liberation. If it is guilt before a just judge, the cure is a just verdict. If it is a corrupted human nature, the cure is a new humanity. The nine theories below are nine answers to that diagnostic question.

sources.author: J. N. D. Kelly
sources.title: Early Christian Doctrines
sources.locator: chapters on the doctrine of redemption

sources.author: Mark D. Baker and Joel B. Green
sources.title: Recovering the Scandal of the Cross

callout.text: Myth: 'The church has always had one official theory of the atonement.' Fact: no ecumenical council defined one. Individual traditions have confessional preferences (for example the Reformed confessions favour penal substitution and the Catholic Council of Trent speaks of Christ's satisfaction), but these are not shared by all Christians.

sections.heading: The early church: recapitulation, ransom and healing
sections.body:
Recapitulation comes from Irenaeus of Lyons around AD 180. His word means 'summing up again'. Adam failed and dragged humanity down with him; Christ, the second Adam, goes back over the whole human story and gets it right at every stage: born, tempted, obedient where Adam disobeyed, even to death. By living the human life faithfully he becomes the new head of a renewed humanity.

The ransom theory, found in Origen in the third century and Gregory of Nyssa in the fourth, starts from Jesus' saying that he came 'to give his life as a ransom for many'. Humanity had sold itself into the devil's power. Christ gave himself as the price. Some writers added vivid pictures: Gregory of Nyssa compared Christ's humanity to bait hiding the hook of his divinity, so death swallowed what it could not hold. Others, such as Gregory of Nazianzus, rejected the idea that any price was paid to the devil at all.

The healing or participatory view, strongest in Athanasius and the Eastern Fathers, treats sin above all as corruption and death spreading through human nature. The Word of God took a full human nature in order to heal it from the inside. Athanasius's famous summary is that God became human so that humans might be made sharers in the divine life. Eastern Orthodox churches still read the cross mainly this way: within the incarnation and resurrection, as the cure of death.

callout.text: Myth: 'The early Fathers thought God paid the devil a fee.' Some used ransom language that way, but the Fathers disagreed among themselves, and Gregory of Nazianzus explicitly called a payment to the devil an outrage. For most, 'ransom' was a picture of liberation, not a literal transaction.

sections.heading: Christus Victor: the cross as victory
sections.body:
In 1931 the Swedish bishop Gustaf Aulén published *Christus Victor*. He argued that the main view of the early church, and of Martin Luther, was not a theory about paying anything but a drama of battle. Humanity is held captive by sin, death and the devil. Christ enters the battle, appears to lose on the cross, and then triumphs in the resurrection, freeing the captives.

Aulén called this the 'classic' view. Its favourite texts are those where Christ 'disarmed the rulers and authorities' and destroys 'the works of the devil'. Supporters like it because it gives the resurrection a central role, takes evil powers seriously, and fits the Gospel stories of Jesus casting out demons and binding the 'strong man'.

Today it is popular across many traditions, from Orthodox writers to Anabaptists such as J. Denny Weaver and Gregory Boyd. Some versions keep penal substitution alongside; others, especially 'narrative Christus Victor', present it as a replacement for any idea of punishment.

callout.text: Historians question Aulén's history. Critics say he simplified the Fathers and read Luther selectively, since Luther also uses strong substitution language. Defenders reply that victory over the powers really is the dominant early image even if it was never the only one.

sections.heading: Satisfaction: Anselm and God's honour
sections.body:
Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, finished *Why God Became Man* (Cur Deus Homo) in 1098. He wanted to explain the cross by reason, in a way that did not involve the devil having any rights.

His argument runs like this. Sin is a failure to give God the honour he is due. Simply waving it away would leave the moral order of the universe broken. Either the honour is restored (satisfaction) or punishment follows. Humanity owes the debt but cannot pay it, because everything we could offer we already owe. Only God could pay it, but only a human ought to. So God becomes human. Christ, who owed no death because he was sinless, freely gives his life, an offering of infinite worth that more than restores God's honour. The surplus merit flows to those united to him.

Anselm's world was feudal: honour and obligation held society together. Critics say he took over feudal categories; defenders say he was explaining a biblical point about God's holiness in the language of his day. Thomas Aquinas refined the view, and satisfaction remains the main framework in Catholic teaching.

sources.author: Anselm of Canterbury
sources.title: Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man)

callout.text: Myth: 'Anselm taught that Christ was punished in our place.' Anselm actually set satisfaction and punishment as alternatives: Christ's gift of honour means punishment is not needed. Penal substitution is a later, different view, though it borrowed from Anselm.

sections.heading: Moral influence: Abelard and the power of love
sections.body:
Peter Abelard, a Paris teacher, wrote a commentary on Romans in the 1130s. At Romans 3:26 he asked how the death of an innocent could please God. His answer stressed what the cross does to us: in Christ's death God shows such love that our hearts are set on fire, and that love frees us from fear and moves us to love him back.

The nineteenth century turned this into a full theory. Friedrich Schleiermacher, Horace Bushnell and Hastings Rashdall held that the cross changes people, not God. God was never unwilling to forgive; what blocks reconciliation is our hard heart, and the sight of self-giving love melts it.

The view rests on real texts: 'God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us' (Romans 5:8), and 'the love of Christ controls us' (2 Corinthians 5:14). Almost every Christian tradition agrees that the cross does this. The question is whether this is all it does.

sources.author: Peter Abelard
sources.title: Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans

sources.author: Hastings Rashdall
sources.title: The Idea of Atonement in Christian Theology

callout.text: Myth: 'Abelard reduced the cross to a good example.' His commentary also speaks of Christ bearing our sins and of redemption. Historians such as Richard Weingart argue the 'mere example' reading is a later caricature. The purely subjective theory belongs more to nineteenth-century liberal theology than to Abelard himself.

sections.heading: Penal substitution: Christ bears the penalty
sections.body:
Penal substitution was set out systematically by the Reformers, especially John Calvin, and developed by later Reformed theologians such as Francis Turretin and Charles Hodge. In the twentieth century John Stott's *The Cross of Christ* (1986) and J. I. Packer's lecture 'What Did the Cross Achieve?' (1973) became its classic modern defences.

The view says: God is holy and just, sin deserves death, and God will not pretend it does not. Out of love, God the Son freely takes the place of sinners and bears the penalty they deserved: condemnation, the curse, separation. Because the penalty has been borne, God can forgive and declare sinners righteous while remaining just. Its key texts are Isaiah 53 ('the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all'), 2 Corinthians 5:21, Galatians 3:13 and Romans 3:25-26.

Most evangelical and Reformed confessions treat it as central. Defenders argue it is the only theory that explains why Jesus had to die rather than merely could, and why the Bible speaks of God's wrath being turned away. They also stress that the Father and Son act together: it is God himself, not an innocent third party, who bears the cost.

sources.author: J. I. Packer
sources.title: What Did the Cross Achieve? The Logic of Penal Substitution (Tyndale Bulletin 25)

sources.author: Steve Jeffery, Michael Ovey and Andrew Sach
sources.title: Pierced for Our Transgressions

callout.text: Myth: 'Penal substitution means an angry Father punishing an unwilling Son' (critics have called it 'cosmic child abuse'). Its defenders reject this: the Son is willing (John 10:18), the Father acts out of love (John 3:16), and the Trinity acts as one. Critics reply that the problem remains if one person of the Trinity punishes another. Separately, defenders point to earlier hints (for example Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel* 10.1), while critics say the full theory is a Reformation creation; that historical question is still argued.

sections.heading: Governmental: the cross upholds God's moral order
sections.body:
Hugo Grotius, a Dutch lawyer and theologian, wrote in 1617 to defend Christ's satisfaction against Socinian critics. He pictured God less as a creditor or offended party and more as the just ruler of the universe. A ruler can relax a law, but cannot simply ignore lawbreaking without undermining the law itself.

On this view Christ's death was not an exact payment of the penalty each sinner owed. It was a public demonstration of how seriously God takes sin, which makes it safe for God to forgive without weakening his moral government. Romans 3:25-26, where God shows his righteousness 'at the present time', is its key text.

The view was taken up by the New England theologians after Jonathan Edwards, by the revivalist Charles Finney, and by many Methodist and Wesleyan writers such as John Miley. It suits Arminian theology because it fits an atonement made for all people without automatically securing anyone's salvation.

sources.author: Hugo Grotius
sources.title: Defensio fidei catholicae de satisfactione Christi

sections.heading: Mimetic (scapegoat): exposing human violence
sections.body:
The French literary critic René Girard (1923-2015) argued that human cultures hold together by a hidden mechanism. People imitate each other's desires, rivalry spreads, and tension is released by uniting against a victim, a scapegoat, whose death brings peace and is later treated as sacred.

Girard believed the Gospels unmask this mechanism. Jesus is the innocent victim the crowd, the priests and the Romans unite against; Caiaphas even says it is better for one man to die for the people. But unlike ancient myths, the Gospels tell the story from the victim's side and declare him innocent, and God vindicates him in the resurrection. Once the lie is exposed, the cycle of sacred violence loses its power.

Theologians such as Raymund Schwager, James Alison and S. Mark Heim have built Girard's insight into an atonement theology. It speaks powerfully to questions of violence, scapegoating and religious persecution.

sources.author: René Girard
sources.title: Things Hidden Since the Foundation of the World

sources.author: René Girard
sources.title: I See Satan Fall Like Lightning

sections.heading: One centre or many pictures?
sections.body:
Since about 2000 many writers have stressed that the Bible's atonement language is a 'kaleidoscope': each image shows something true, and no single theory can carry everything. Mark Baker and Joel Green made this case in *Recovering the Scandal of the Cross*; Scot McKnight compared the theories to clubs in a golf bag, each suited to a different shot.

Others argue that the pictures need a centre. Many evangelicals say penal substitution is the 'heart' that makes the others work: Christ defeats the powers precisely by removing the guilt that gave them their grip (Colossians 2:14-15). Some Christus Victor writers say victory is the frame and substitution one tactic within it. Orthodox theologians tend to place everything inside the incarnation and the defeat of death.

For a reader, a useful habit is to ask of any theory: what does it think the problem is, does Scripture name that problem, and does the theory leave out something Scripture clearly says?

sources.author: Fleming Rutledge
sources.title: The Crucifixion: Understanding the Death of Jesus Christ

sources.author: Henri Blocher
sources.title: 'Agnus Victor: The Atonement as Victory and Vicarious Punishment', in What Does It Mean to Be Saved?

views.name: One central model
views.summary: Many Reformed and evangelical writers hold that penal substitution is the heart of the atonement and the other images depend on it; some Christus Victor writers argue the same for victory.

views.name: Kaleidoscope or plural models
views.summary: Writers such as Joel Green, Mark Baker and Scot McKnight hold that Scripture deliberately uses many images and no one theory should dominate.

views.name: Incarnational frame (Orthodox)
views.summary: Eastern Orthodox theology places the cross inside the whole story of incarnation, death and resurrection, and reads salvation chiefly as healing and union with God.

title: Retributive and Restorative Justice
question: When the Bible says God is just, does it mean he punishes wrongdoing as it deserves, or that he puts things right? And what difference does the answer make?
plainAnswer: 'Retributive' justice means giving wrongdoing the response it deserves: guilt calls for a fitting penalty. 'Restorative' justice means repairing the damage: healing victims, changing offenders and mending broken relationships. The Bible clearly contains both ideas. It speaks of God repaying each person according to their deeds, and it speaks of God's justice as rescuing the poor and making the world whole. Christians disagree over which of these is the deeper meaning, and many argue that in God they are two sides of one justice. The answer changes how people explain the cross, picture the final judgment, and handle sin and conflict in church.
keyTakeaways: The Hebrew words mishpat (justice) and tsedaqah (righteousness) often appear together and cover both judging wrong and rescuing the wronged.
Retributive justice asks 'what does this wrong deserve?'; restorative justice asks 'what will put this right?'
Retributive views tend to support penal substitution; restorative views tend to stress Christus Victor, healing and covenant renewal.
Both views take the final judgment seriously, but they differ on what it is for: vindicating God's righteousness, or completing the healing of creation.
In church life the debate affects discipline, forgiveness, restitution and how Christians engage with criminal justice.
Integrative views (Volf, Keller, Wolterstorff, Rutledge) argue that Scripture refuses to choose between the two.

sections.heading: The words behind 'justice'
sections.body:
English Bibles translate two Hebrew words, mishpat and tsedaqah, as 'justice' and 'righteousness'. They often appear as a pair, as in Amos's cry: 'let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream'.

Mishpat comes from the verb 'to judge' and covers court verdicts, fair rulings and the right order of things. Tsedaqah means being in the right, especially faithfully keeping one's commitments in a relationship. In the Psalms and prophets, God's tsedaqah is very often his saving action: he 'does justice' for the orphan and widow by rescuing them.

The New Testament word dikaiosyne carries both senses. It can mean God's own rightness, the right standing he gives to people, or the right living he produces in them. Paul's phrase 'the righteousness of God' is one of the most debated phrases in the Bible for exactly this reason.

sources.author: Christopher D. Marshall
sources.title: Beyond Retribution: A New Testament Vision for Justice, Crime, and Punishment

sections.heading: Retributive justice in plain words
sections.body:
Retributive comes from a Latin word meaning 'to pay back'. Retributive justice says that wrongdoing deserves a response that fits it. The punishment is not mainly about deterring others or reforming the offender, though it may do both; it is about honouring the truth that a real wrong has been done. A judge who lets the guilty walk free is not being kind but unjust.

Scripture often speaks this way. Abraham asks, 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?' God 'will by no means clear the guilty'. Paul says God 'will render to each one according to his works' and that 'the wages of sin is death'. The angel in Revelation praises God because his judgments are 'true and just'.

Classic defenders include Anselm, Calvin, Charles Hodge, Leon Morris and J. I. Packer. They see God's justice as part of his nature, not a policy he could change. Because God is holy, sin cannot simply be overlooked; it must be dealt with.

sources.author: J. I. Packer
sources.title: Knowing God
sources.locator: chapters on God's judgment and wrath

callout.text: Myth: 'An eye for an eye' was a licence for revenge. In context (Exodus 21, Leviticus 24, Deuteronomy 19) it was a rule for judges, setting a limit: the penalty must not exceed the harm. Jewish practice early on understood many such cases as monetary compensation. Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:38-42 addresses personal retaliation, not the courts.

sections.heading: Restorative justice in plain words
sections.body:
Restorative justice asks a different first question: not 'what does the offender deserve?' but 'who has been hurt, what do they need, and whose job is it to put things right?' The modern movement grew in the 1970s and 1980s, especially among Mennonites working in criminal justice. Howard Zehr's *Changing Lenses* (1990) is its classic text.

Christian defenders argue that this is close to the Bible's own heart. Biblical law required restitution: a thief repaid what he took plus a fifth, or more. Zacchaeus, on meeting Jesus, promised to repay fourfold. The prophets picture justice as the restoration of shalom, wholeness, for the whole community. Christopher Marshall argues that the New Testament's vision of justice is 'restorative' in this sense, and N. T. Wright reads 'the righteousness of God' in Paul as God's faithfulness to his covenant promise to put the world right.

Restorative views do not deny punishment. They argue that where punishment appears in Scripture, it serves a larger goal of repair rather than being an end in itself.

sources.author: Howard Zehr
sources.title: Changing Lenses: A New Focus for Crime and Justice

sources.author: N. T. Wright
sources.title: Paul and the Faithfulness of God

callout.text: Myth: 'Restorative justice means no consequences.' Its defenders insist on accountability: offenders must face the harm done and make amends. What they reject is punishment that does nothing to repair harm.

sections.heading: Holding both together
sections.body:
A third group argues that Scripture never forces a choice. Psalm 85 pictures 'righteousness and peace' kissing each other. Isaiah 11 describes the Messiah judging the poor with fairness and striking the wicked in the same breath.

Miroslav Volf, a Croatian theologian who lived through the Balkan wars, argued in *Exclusion and Embrace* (1996) that belief in God's final judgment is what frees victims to forgive: they do not have to take revenge because God will set things right. Tim Keller's *Generous Justice* (2010) stresses that the God who punishes oppression is the same God who defends the poor. Nicholas Wolterstorff grounds justice in the worth God gives to every person, which makes wrongs both deserve judgment and call for repair. Fleming Rutledge holds penal and victory language together in her study of the cross.

On this view, God judges evil because he loves what evil destroys. Judgment without restoration would be cold; restoration without judgment would pretend the wrong did not matter.

sections.heading: What this means for the cross
sections.body:
If justice is chiefly retributive, the central question of the cross is: how can God forgive sinners and still be just? Paul's answer in Romans 3:26, that God is 'just and the justifier', is read as saying the penalty was really paid. This is the backbone of penal substitution.

If justice is chiefly restorative, the cross is God's decisive act of putting the world right: defeating evil, absorbing violence without returning it, forming a reconciled people, and opening the way to a healed creation. Christus Victor, recapitulation and healing models fit naturally here. Penal language is often reread as describing what sin does to us rather than what God inflicts.

Integrative readers argue that the cross does both. Sin is condemned in the flesh of Christ (Romans 8:3), and in the same act enemies are reconciled and powers disarmed (Colossians 1:20; 2:15).

callout.text: N. T. Wright accepts that Jesus bore the punishment of exile and death for Israel and the world, but places it within a covenant story of God putting the world right. Some Reformed critics, such as John Piper in *The Future of Justification* (2007), argue that his reading of 'righteousness' loses the imputation of Christ's righteousness to believers.

sections.heading: What this means for the final judgment
sections.body:
All mainstream Christian traditions affirm a final judgment: Christ will judge the living and the dead. Scripture describes books opened, people judged by their works, and a separation between the righteous and the wicked.

Retributive readers see the final judgment as God publicly and finally giving each what is due. This usually goes with the traditional view of hell as conscious punishment, though some (conditionalists) argue that the just penalty is final destruction.

Restorative readers emphasise texts about God reconciling all things and making all things new. Some go further, to hopeful or confident universalism, in which even judgment aims at the eventual restoration of the judged. Most restorative writers stop short of that and say judgment is the removal of everything that destroys creation so that the new creation can flourish.

In both views the judgment is good news for victims: the evil done to them will not be ignored.

sections.heading: What this means for church life
sections.body:
Jesus gives a process for dealing with sin in the church: go privately, then with witnesses, then to the church. The goal he names is 'you have gained your brother'. Paul tells the Corinthians to remove a man living in serious sin, but later urges them to forgive and comfort a repentant offender so he is not overwhelmed. Galatians 6:1 says to restore the one caught in sin 'in a spirit of gentleness'.

A strongly retributive instinct can lead churches to stress consequences, protection of the community and clear boundaries. A strongly restorative instinct can lead churches to stress reconciliation, listening to victims and the offender's return. Each has its danger: the first can become harsh and slow to welcome back; the second can push victims to forgive too quickly or leave offenders in positions where they can harm again.

The same debate shapes Christian thinking about prisons, the death penalty and national reconciliation. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was an explicit attempt to apply restorative principles after apartheid.

sources.author: Howard Zehr
sources.title: The Little Book of Restorative Justice

callout.text: Myth: 'Forgiveness means no consequences.' Most traditions distinguish forgiveness (giving up personal revenge and resentment) from trust and from legal consequences. Romans 12:19 forbids personal vengeance; Romans 13:4 still gives the state a role in punishing wrongdoing.

sections.heading: Common misunderstandings
sections.body:
A frequent claim is that the Old Testament God is retributive and the New Testament God restorative. This idea goes back to Marcion in the second century, whom the church rejected. The Old Testament is full of mercy and restoration (Exodus 34:6, Hosea 11, Isaiah 40), and the New Testament contains some of the Bible's sternest warnings of judgment, many from Jesus himself.

Another is that retributive justice is the same as vengeance. Its defenders distinguish them: vengeance is personal, unmeasured and driven by anger; retribution is impartial, proportionate and carried out by rightful authority.

A third is that restorative justice is a secular or liberal import. Its modern form grew largely from Mennonite Christian practice, and its defenders argue its roots are in the biblical laws of restitution and the prophetic vision of shalom.

What would a church discipline process look like that took both views seriously?
How does 'the righteousness of God' in Romans 1:17 change if it means covenant faithfulness?

title: Every Prophet and Apostle in the Bible
question: Who were the prophets and apostles of the Bible, what did each one say or do, and what happened to them?
plainAnswer: A prophet in the Bible is someone who speaks for God, usually to warn, call people back to faithfulness, or announce what God is about to do. Sixteen prophets have books named after them, but dozens more appear in the stories, including several women, and the New Testament names prophets too. The Bible also names false prophets and gives tests for spotting them. An apostle is someone 'sent' with authority: above all the Twelve whom Jesus chose, plus Paul and a handful of others the New Testament also calls apostles. The Bible tells us how only a few of them died; most of what people 'know' about the deaths of the apostles comes from later tradition, which ranges from early and fairly reliable to late and legendary.
keyTakeaways: 'Major' and 'minor' prophets refers to the length of their books, not their importance.
Some of the most important prophets, such as Elijah, Elisha, Nathan and Samuel, wrote no book.
The Bible names women prophets in both Testaments: Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, Isaiah's wife, Anna and Philip's four daughters.
The four lists of the Twelve agree on the core but differ on one or two names, mainly Thaddaeus / Judas son of James.
The New Testament also calls Paul, Barnabas, James the Lord's brother, Andronicus and Junia apostles, among others.

The Bible records the deaths of only James son of Zebedee and Judas Iscariot among the Twelve; the deaths of Peter, Paul and James the Lord's brother are well attested outside the Bible; most other stories are later tradition.

sections.heading: What a prophet was
sections.body:
The usual Hebrew word for prophet is navi, probably meaning 'one who is called' or 'one who calls out'. Older terms were ro'eh and hozeh, both meaning 'seer'; 1 Samuel notes that 'he who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer'. Prophets were also called 'man of God'.

The clearest definition comes from God's words about Aaron: 'he shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him', and later 'Aaron your brother shall be your prophet'. A prophet is God's spokesperson. Deuteronomy says God will put his words in the prophet's mouth.

Predicting the future was only part of the job. Most prophetic speech is about the present: calling kings and people back to the covenant, condemning injustice and idolatry, and announcing judgment or hope as a result. Scholars sometimes put it as 'forth-telling' more than 'fore-telling'.

The full lists are in the in-app roster at /rosters?r=prophets.

sections.heading: The major prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel
sections.body:
Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem from about 740 to 700 BC, under kings Uzziah to Hezekiah. He warned Judah against trusting Assyria and Egypt instead of God, and announced a coming king and a suffering servant. Many scholars think chapters 40-66 come from later disciples speaking to exiles; traditional readers hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book.

Jeremiah prophesied from 627 BC until after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC. He told Judah that Babylon would win and that surrender was God's will, which got him beaten, imprisoned and thrown into a cistern. He also promised a new covenant written on the heart. The Bible last sees him taken to Egypt against his will.

Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon in 597 BC. From about 593 to 571 BC he spoke to the exiles in strange visions and acted-out signs: God's glory leaving the temple, a valley of dry bones coming to life, and a new temple.

Daniel served in the Babylonian and Persian courts from 605 to about 536 BC. His book combines court stories with visions of empires and a coming kingdom of God. Jewish Bibles place it among the Writings rather than the Prophets, and many scholars date the final book to about 165 BC; traditional readers hold to the sixth century.

callout.text: Myth: 'The minor prophets are less important.' The labels come from Augustine's time and refer only to length. The twelve shorter books were copied on a single scroll in Jewish tradition, called 'the Twelve'.

sections.heading: The Twelve 'minor' prophets
sections.body:
Hosea (about 755-715 BC) spoke to the northern kingdom, Israel. God told him to marry an unfaithful wife as a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness and God's persistent love.

Amos (about 760 BC) was a shepherd and fig farmer from Tekoa in Judah sent north to Israel. He attacked luxury built on the backs of the poor. Jonah (about 780 BC) was the reluctant prophet sent to Nineveh; 2 Kings mentions him under Jeroboam II. Micah (about 735-700 BC) spoke to both Samaria and Jerusalem about injustice and named Bethlehem as the ruler's birthplace.

Nahum (between 663 and 612 BC) announced the fall of Nineveh. Zephaniah (about 630 BC, under Josiah) warned of the 'day of the LORD'. Habakkuk (about 605 BC) argued with God over why Babylon was allowed to triumph and learned that 'the righteous shall live by his faith'. Obadiah (after 586 BC) condemned Edom for joining in Jerusalem's fall.

After the exile, Haggai and Zechariah (520-518 BC) urged the returned exiles to rebuild the temple, and Malachi (about 450 BC) rebuked careless priests and promised the return of Elijah. Joel cannot be dated with confidence; suggestions range from the ninth to the fourth century BC. He described a locust plague and promised the Spirit poured out on all flesh.

callout.text: Dates for Joel, Obadiah and Malachi are educated guesses based on content. The book of Jonah is read by many scholars as a didactic story rather than a report; traditional readers take it as history, noting that Jesus refers to Jonah (Matthew 12:39-41).

sections.heading: Prophets who wrote no book
sections.body:
Many of the Bible's prophets never wrote a book, or their writings are lost. The earliest are figures not usually thought of as prophets: Enoch (according to Jude), Abraham (whom God calls a prophet), Moses, the greatest prophet in the Old Testament's own estimate, and his brother Aaron.

In the days of the judges and early kings we meet Deborah, an unnamed prophet in Gideon's day, Samuel, Gad (David's seer), and Nathan, who rebuked David over Bathsheba. In the divided kingdom we meet Ahijah of Shiloh, Shemaiah, the man of God from Judah, Iddo the seer, Jehu son of Hanani and his father Hanani, Azariah son of Oded, Micaiah son of Imlah, Jahaziel, Eliezer son of Dodavahu, Zechariah son of Jehoiada (stoned in the temple court), Oded of Samaria, and the great pair Elijah and Elisha.

Chronicles also says that the temple musicians Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun 'prophesied' with lyres and cymbals, and it mentions prophetic records by Nathan, Gad, Iddo and others that have not survived. Late in the monarchy Uriah son of Shemaiah prophesied like Jeremiah and was executed by King Jehoiakim.

sections.heading: Women prophets
sections.body:
The Bible names women prophets in both Testaments. Miriam, Moses' sister, is called a prophetess and led Israel's song after the Red Sea crossing. Deborah was a prophetess and judge who summoned Barak to battle. Huldah was consulted by King Josiah's officials when the Book of the Law was found in the temple; her word confirmed coming judgment and set off Josiah's reform. Isaiah's wife is called 'the prophetess', though whether that means she prophesied or simply was the prophet's wife is debated.

In the New Testament, Anna, an elderly widow, is called a prophetess and spoke about the infant Jesus to all who were waiting for redemption. Philip the evangelist had four unmarried daughters who prophesied. Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy in church gatherings, and Peter's Pentecost sermon applies Joel's promise that 'your sons and your daughters shall prophesy'.

The Bible also names false prophetesses: Noadiah, who opposed Nehemiah; women who 'prophesy out of their own hearts' in Ezekiel; and the woman Jesus calls 'Jezebel' in Thyatira.

callout.text: Jewish tradition in the Talmud (Megillah 14a) counts seven prophetesses of Israel: Sarah, Miriam, Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah and Esther. Only Miriam, Deborah and Huldah are called prophetesses in the Hebrew Bible itself.

sections.heading: New Testament prophets
sections.body:
Luke's opening chapters are full of prophecy: Zechariah the priest prophesied at his son's birth, Simeon spoke over the baby Jesus in the temple, and Anna gave thanks. John the Baptist, Jesus said, was a prophet and 'more than a prophet', the messenger Malachi had promised.

Jesus himself was recognised as a prophet by the crowds and was called the prophet like Moses by Peter. He said a prophet is not without honour except in his home town.

In the early church, prophets were a recognised group. Prophets from Jerusalem came to Antioch, and one of them, Agabus, predicted a famine and later Paul's arrest. The church at Antioch had 'prophets and teachers': Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen and Saul. Judas Barsabbas and Silas were prophets who encouraged the church after the Jerusalem council. Paul lists prophets second after apostles and gives rules for testing prophecy in church. The author of Revelation calls his book 'the words of this prophecy'.

callout.text: Christians disagree on whether New Testament prophecy carried the same authority as Old Testament prophecy. Wayne Grudem argues it was a fallible report of what the Spirit brought to mind, to be weighed; Richard Gaffin and others argue it was revelatory and has ceased now that the canon is complete. See /debates/cessationism.

sections.heading: False prophets and how to spot them
sections.body:
The Bible takes false prophecy seriously. Deuteronomy gives two tests: a prophet who leads people after other gods is false even if his sign comes true, and a prophet whose prediction fails has not spoken from the LORD. Jesus adds a third: 'you will recognise them by their fruits'. John adds a fourth: whether a spirit confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

Named false prophets include Balaam (who blessed Israel under God's control but later led Israel into sin), the 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah on Mount Carmel, the old prophet of Bethel who lied to the man of God, Zedekiah son of Chenaanah who struck Micaiah, Hananiah son of Azur who broke Jeremiah's yoke, Pashhur, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, Shemaiah the Nehelamite, Noadiah and Shemaiah son of Delaiah who tried to frighten Nehemiah, Bar-Jesus (Elymas) on Cyprus, 'Jezebel' at Thyatira, and the 'false prophet' of Revelation.

Some of these figures are complicated. Balaam really did receive words from God, and the old prophet of Bethel later spoke a true word of judgment. The Bible treats prophecy as something that must always be tested.

sections.heading: The Twelve apostles and their names
sections.body:
Apostolos in Greek means 'someone sent'. Jesus chose twelve from his wider group of disciples, a number that echoes the twelve tribes of Israel. The New Testament lists them four times, and the lists vary in small ways, mostly because people had several names.

Simon was renamed Cephas (Aramaic) or Peter (Greek), both meaning 'rock'. James and John, sons of Zebedee, were nicknamed Boanerges, 'sons of thunder'. Thomas was also called Didymus, 'twin'. Matthew the tax collector appears as Levi son of Alphaeus in Mark and Luke's call stories, and most readers take them as the same man. Simon is called 'the Cananaean' (KJV 'Canaanite') in Matthew and Mark, from an Aramaic word for 'zealous', and 'the Zealot' in Luke and Acts.

The main puzzle is the tenth name. Matthew and Mark have Thaddaeus (some manuscripts of Matthew have Lebbaeus); Luke and Acts have Judas of James, usually translated 'son of James' (KJV 'brother of James'). John's Gospel mentions 'Judas, not Iscariot'. Most readers think these are one person with two names. John never gives a list and never names Bartholomew, but he features Nathanael, whom later tradition identified with Bartholomew.

After Judas Iscariot's death the eleven chose Matthias by lot to restore the number to twelve. See /rosters?r=apostles.

sources.author: Bruce M. Metzger
sources.title: A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament

callout.text: Myth: 'The Bible says Bartholomew and Nathanael are the same person.' It does not. The identification is a later suggestion based on John pairing Nathanael with Philip, as the lists pair Bartholomew with Philip. It is plausible but unproven.

sections.heading: Others called apostles
sections.body:
The New Testament uses 'apostle' in a narrow and a wider sense. In the narrow sense, an apostle had seen the risen Lord and been commissioned by him. Paul insists he meets that test, though 'as one untimely born'.

Besides the Twelve and Paul, the New Testament calls these people apostles: Barnabas (with Paul in Acts 14); James the Lord's brother (Galatians 1:19, depending on how the verse is read); Andronicus and Junia, who are 'of note among the apostles'; and, in 1 Thessalonians, probably Silas and Timothy as well as Paul. Epaphroditus is called the Philippians' 'messenger' (apostolos), and Paul speaks of 'messengers (apostoloi) of the churches', meaning sent delegates. Hebrews even calls Jesus 'the apostle and high priest of our confession'.

Paul also warns of 'false apostles' and 'super-apostles' at Corinth, and Revelation praises the Ephesians for testing those who called themselves apostles and were not.

callout.text: Romans 16:7: was Junia a woman, and was she 'well known among the apostles' (an apostle herself) or 'well known to the apostles' (respected by them)? Most scholars now accept she was a woman, as John Chrysostom assumed when he praised her. The second question is still argued; Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace (2001) argued for 'to the apostles', and others, including Epp, have replied.

sections.heading: What happened to the apostles: Bible and tradition
sections.body:
The Bible records very little. James son of Zebedee was killed with the sword by Herod Agrippa I around AD 44, the first of the Twelve to die. Judas Iscariot died after the betrayal; Matthew says he hanged himself and Acts says he fell headlong and burst open, two accounts that have been harmonised in different ways. Jesus foretold that Peter would be led where he did not want to go, 'to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God'. Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome, and 2 Timothy has him expecting death.

Outside the Bible, three deaths are well attested. Peter and Paul died in Rome under Nero in the mid-60s (1 Clement, about AD 96, refers to their witness and suffering; later writers add that Peter was crucified and Paul beheaded). James the Lord's brother was stoned in Jerusalem in AD 62, according to the Jewish historian Josephus.

For most of the others we depend on later tradition of mixed quality. Early writers say John lived to old age in Ephesus. Thomas is linked with Parthia and India, Andrew with Scythia and Greece, Philip with Hierapolis, Bartholomew with India and Armenia. Stories of how each died, such as Andrew's X-shaped cross or Bartholomew being flayed, come mostly from apocryphal Acts written from the late second century onward, or from much later martyr lists.

callout.text: Myth: 'Every apostle except John died a martyr, and we know how.' The Bible records only James's martyrdom (and Judas's death). Peter, Paul and James the Lord's brother are well attested. For most others, the martyrdom stories are late and sometimes contradictory, and Clement of Alexandria preserves a second-century source (Heracleon) saying Matthew, Philip and Thomas did not die as martyrs. Sean McDowell's careful study rates each apostle's case separately.
